utterances.text: Your Honours, briefly before the break, before we take the next pause, last week Mr. Lukic during direct examination used an organigram depicting the structure of the Main Staff of the VRS with General Skrbic. With your leave, I'd like to ask the usher to please provide the B/C/S version on the ELMO so that -- I have one question that I'd like to ask General Skrbic about this structure, please. And if you could show it to Mr. Lukic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you saw this organigram last week. You made some corrections to it. It's an attempt to describe or to depict the structure of the VRS Main Staff in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, perhaps, or with our audio/visual people, can we please zoom in on the bottom right corner of this document, please. The bottom right quarter -- no, now we're going to -- no, sorry, the other way, we need to go the other way. Can we please move the document to the left, please. More to the left, please. Okay. Now stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you stop it right there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- you'll see at the very bottom of the page there is a square that says "10th Sabotage Detachment." Do you see that? General Skrbic, can you look at the hard copy in front of you. It's probably going to be much clearer. It's this box right here.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment was part of the structure of the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But it was not called the 10th Sabotage Detachment, but rather the 10th Reconnaissance Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And so as part of the structure of the VRS Main Staff, the 10th Reconnaissance Sabotage Detachment would have been subordinated to General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we take the second break now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly can we show the witness again Exhibit P1934.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I'm going to take you back for a few moments to the personnel file of Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 11 in the B/C/S version, please, and to the next page in the English version, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, maybe just to orient you, if you could please first take a look at the entry where Colonel Popovic is assigned to the security administration of the 30th Personnel Centre, and this is the particular order dated 30 September 1998. Do you see that? It's in the middle of the page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm not receiving -- or actually, I don't have the English translation on the left-hand side screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this -- if we look at the entry above it, we see that Colonel Popovic is assigned to the 30th Personnel Centre, a duty station not determined, and that's dated the 3rd of July, 1998. And then the next entry Colonel Popovic, he's assigned to the security administration of the 30th Personnel Centre dated the 30th of September, 1998. Even though those entries say the 30th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the VJ, it really means that Colonel Popovic was serving in the VRS; right? De facto now, de facto.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And then in the next entry it says that Colonel Popovic was sent or perhaps by now General Popovic was sent temporarily to the 2nd Army of the VJ. This is the entry of the 22nd April 1999. And so in this appointment General Popovic is going to be serving de facto and de jure in the Army of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Popovic never became a general. He -- he's a colonel. However, judging from the wording, I cannot conclude that he was de facto in a different army -- the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to come back to this in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, can you remind us what the headings to the various columns are because we talk of assigned -- looking at the first column and then we talk of assigned looking at the second column as well. I'm not quite sure what is happening in each of these columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the English version can we please go back a page. And if we could focus a bit on the upper part of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Status in service. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unit - institution and place. Okay. That doesn't tell us much. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, Skrbic -- whoa, what just happened there. Can we go back to what we saw before. General Skrbic, what does status in the service of the active military serviceman mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Status in the service implies an establishment duty, a rank that is required for such an establishment duty, the pay group, and the time from which to which that duty is performed. Those are the facts that give rise to the status that you have inquired about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- some other elements that at this point in time are not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next column to the right is entitled "unit - institution and place," and that's pretty self-explanatory, isn't it? It refers to the particular unit within a particular institution of an army where the person is assigned and the particular place; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm reading in that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then the next column over to the right, "establishment rank - training and occupational specialty," which we see in these columns it's often a series of numbers, but we see it refers to the rank of the person and the particular professional training or professional specialisation that the officer has; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it also would include a pay grade, right, for PG?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're reading it PJ and I'm reading it PG, and in any case it stands for a P group or a P grade, but they're both the same, are they not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I tried to say PG, but obviously I didn't speak very clearly. My mistake. What does rank grouping mean? It's the next column over. What does the phrase rank grouping --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The time is self-explanatory and then the last column on the right, "decree-order which regulated the status," refers to the particular order that discusses the particular appointment, right, to a particular post?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go back to Exhibit P1934, please.

utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this entry really means that Colonel Popovic is de facto serving in the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, yes. When I say "this" I mean the date, the 1st of July, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does MP mean, if you know, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour, that means according to peace time establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can leave this document, please, and I'd like to move on to another topic. Can we please show the witness Exhibit D347.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, you saw this document during your direct examination. And it says here that your -- you would be relieved of your duties as -- effective 31 January 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm reading, Mr. Saxon, but that's not correct. It should have been the 31st of January, 1996 -- oh, I apologise. I apologise. It's correct. Everything's correct. Whatever you have read out is correct and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No problem. No need to apologise. All right. Now, last Thursday during your direct examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 11808 of the transcript, lines 6 to 7 or a bit before that starting at page 11807.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- you described the work that you did in the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff from 1997 until 2000 in the capacity of a stand-in. And you explained that you assisted the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the interpreter and I understand the interpreter when Mr. Saxon said you were standing -- I believe that Mr. Saxon meant acting on somebody's behalf, not physically standing on one's feet. So I just wanted to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And so is the transcript because the transcript said "stand-in," which means exactly that, not you are standing physically there, but that you are standing-in for somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You explain that you assisted the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff on personnel issues in the 30th Personnel Centre. And on page 11808 you told the Trial Chamber: "I did not have an obligation to report to work every day, but nevertheless I did come every day." So just so that I understand you, your position is, sir, that once you were assigned as a stand-in to that position in the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff, you did not have a duty to come to work each day and attend to the daily responsibilities required by the job. That's your position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show General Skrbic P1688.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I want to review with you some portions of your personnel file from the Army of Yugoslavia, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could please start with page 5 from the English excerpt 0611-5200 and page 7 in the B/C/S original. Is there a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the English translation ends with 5205. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is, you'll see, the first page of your personnel file, General Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5 of this English portion, please, and go to page 7 in B/C/S? We can't? Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have. You have the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please try -- and you found it for me. I am most grateful to our courtroom personnel and their superb skill that they're showing today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the court record, reference for the English translation is 0611-5209. Thank you. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, please focus for now on the very first entry where it says, at least in English, "assigned as stand-in." It's an order -- on the right-hand column it reflects an order of the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff dated the 13th of January, 1997. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My first question for you is: How is it that the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff issued an order assigning you as a stand-in in a vacant post in the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff 15 days before President Plavsic issued a decree terminating your service in the VRS? How did that happen? Help us with that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because Mrs. Plavsic told me orally that I could go wherever I wanted to. She thanked me. And subsequently I went to the VJ and reported to them. After that, when she had time enough and when she had the proper documents prepared, she signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well -- but doesn't this demonstrate that concurrently you were subject to the powers and authorities of both the VJ and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you returned to work in the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff, you did not re-enlist in the VJ, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you another portion of your professional -- of your personnel file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can I just ask a question on this one. This very entry, Mr. Skrbic, that has been -- you have been referred to, it says you're performing those duties of stand-in in addition to your regular duties in the period between 10th January and -- to 9th January 1997. What were your other regular duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have spotted that correctly, but in fact I didn't have any other duties. This bureaucratic formulation allows for this kind of wording. Because I had the rank of general, I could not be appointed by any other document other than an order, otherwise a decree on my appointment should have been issued. In my previous testimony I said that not a single member of the VRS was given a decree on appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then that nullifies my next question. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before I show you another portion of your personnel file, I want to remain on this page for another moment, sir. If we just look at the first entry where you're assigned as stand-in and the -- although the dates are different, the language is virtually the same. The first entry from 13 January -- related to the order of 13 January 1997 says: "Assigned as stand-in for the deserted FM ..." FM means establishment post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Assigned as stand-in for the deserted FM," establishment post, "of assistant chief of the personnel administration for the 30th personnel centre, FC Major-General, PG-5, Belgrade garrison." And then it says: "He shall perform the stand-in duties in addition to his regular duties ..." Now, that phrase "he shall perform the stand-in duties ..." confirms that in this particular position you had duties to perform, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had certain duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One of those duties would have been then to come to work and take care of your responsibilities; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to please move to -- in the same exhibit but in a different English translation excerpt, if we could go to English excerpt that has the ERN 0611-5218, and I'm praying that I'm giving the number correctly now. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, here we see the assessment of your work within the VJ -- or certainly an assessment produced by the VJ for the period 30 April 1993 to 30 December 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period of assessment starts on the 26th March 1999 until 28th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We are in -- I'm sorry, we are in the wrong document. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the English translation excerpt before this one -- hold on, hold on. The -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The document that's on our screen, General -- okay, we have an English -- we have an English version assessing the period from 30 April 1993 to 30 December 1998, but in B/C/S we see the period beginning 26 March 1999. General, I'm going to give you a hard copy of the B/C/S version of this assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the ERN number of the B/C/S exists in e-court, and that's 0611-5218.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. We found the right document now. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, General Skrbic, you can see that this is your -- the assessment that was made regarding yourself in the VJ. The period being assessed is the 20 -- now something has gone awry again. I need the English version that we had before, and I can give General Skrbic a hard copy of his version if that would speed things up because -- okay. Now we have -- no, we don't have the right B/C/S version. I'm going to -- okay -- now we have it and I'm grateful to the courtroom personnel for their assistance. Now, General, hopefully you will see your professional assessment from the period of 30 April 1993 to 30 December 1998. Do you see that in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we look down in the middle of the page in both versions, there is a -- there is an item that says post and position in service in the period being assessed. And below that it says assistant commander in the 30th Personnel Centre, assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel at the 30th Personnel Centre of the General Staff. And then it says: "And assistant chief of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff for the 30th Personnel Centre." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I help you with something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please. Okay it's gone now. I'm just looking at those two positions. Both have personnel as a common denominator. What does this mean? Does this mean this is the same thing by a different name or are these two different administrations? The one is commander organisation, mobilisation, and personnel --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next one is assistant chief of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff for the 30th Personnel Centre, which corresponds, for example, to the assignment on stand-in that we saw a moment ago, Your Honour. I can clarify it with the witness if you want, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that you say "for," okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we move forward two pages in the English and one page in Serbo-Croat, please. And can we focus on the bottom of the page, please, in English, the last half of the page in B/C/S. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The description there, General Skrbic, begins this way: "Descriptive assessment and conclusion: As a highly educated and experienced officer and proven patriot, he was selected and dispatched on 17 December 1993 to the 30th Personnel Centre, where he was assigned high-level and responsible duties. Due to his excellent results and achievements, he was promoted to the rank of major-general on 27 December 1995." And then it says: "He confirmed his exceptional qualities as an officer at his post as assistant chief of the personnel administration at the 30th Personnel Centre that he has held since 13 January 1997 ..." I'm not quite sure if that English translation is really precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's "at" or "for."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It should have been assistant chief of the personnel administration for the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And down below in what is in English I think in both versions, the penultimate paragraph: "As a result of these high professional, expert, and moral qualities and his sense for working and managing people, he should continue to hold high military duties at the service." So this assessment is a recognition of the excellent job that you did in carrying out your duties in that position as stand-in; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, although there's some exaggeration and I'm a bit embarrassed by all these attributes and compliments, but I did sign this which meant that I did agree with that eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you're too modest, you're too modest. One thing I'd like to ask you, though, this assessment, it covers the period April 1993 through December 1998. Now, during that period you were serving in the VJ army and then you went to serve in the VRS army and then you came back to serve in the VJ army; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the officer who is signing off on this assessment is assessing you for your period of service or your periods of service in both armies; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period between the 17th December until the date in 1995, I didn't have the assessment of the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps and the commander of the VRS who were in charge of providing an assessment for that particular period. Instead, this gentleman covered that period as well in his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. "This gentleman" being Lieutenant-General Dusan Zoric, the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, can we please show the witness what I hope is the next English portion that hopefully has the ERN range 0611-5216 to 5217. Okay so far so good in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still have "at" instead of "for." The question is how do we interpret all these documents together?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence agrees, I can seek a change -- a revision of the English translation, given the witness's testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, this is very important to be checked in. We should not burden the whole CLSS to translate the entire document or could we just state it for the record that this proposition -- preposition is wrong. And I agree that we should have "for" instead of "at," because that's how it reads in the original. If we state that for the record, I don't see any need for sending the document back to the translation service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We'll do as you suggest, now that you agree that it is supposed to be "for" and not "at." So we'll read it to mean "for."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, in front of you now is your assessment by the VJ for the period of 30 December 1990 -- excuse me, for the period 26 March 1999 to 28 June 1999. And we all know that was war time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was my second war in my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please move forward two pages in English and go forward one page in Serbo-Croat, please. And if we could focus on the bottom half of each page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, in the description that's given here of your performance during this difficult time, it begins: "During the war, with his conduct, behaviour, and steadfastness, especially during enemy attacks on features in the direct vicinity of the troops' deployment, he had a positive influence on the overall success of the forces he commanded." And in the next paragraph it says the following: "He selected officers properly and quickly from the 30th Personnel Centre in order to dispatch them to units and installations focusing on carrying out combat tasks." Now, you've told us before there's nothing in the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska that provides for the transfer of soldiers to the army of a foreign country. So you are able to perform this function as you did during the period of NATO bombing, 1999, you were able to select officers quickly from the 30th Personnel Centre and dispatch them because, at least in a formal sense, those officers were still members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely correct, Mr. Saxon. Do you want me to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief. I will be brief. There is no mystery there at all. At that time there were ten officers in the school for National Defence, and in the command staff school for tactics there were 30 officers I believe. And during their education on the strength of the Army of Yugoslavia, although they were from the Army of Republika Srpska -- and I did nothing else but propose as to where those officers could be assigned in Serbia and Montenegro in terms of their military specialties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you were able to assign them, you were able to assign these officers, because at least in a formal sense these officers were still members of the Army of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both de facto and de jure while they were in education, they did belong to the Army of Yugoslavia. You will remember that I have already told you that we had students from Russia and from France, and when they were educated by the Army of Yugoslavia they were considered to be members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that when a soldier from a foreign -- or an officer from a foreign country comes to participate in an educational activity or an educational programme in the Army of Yugoslavia, that officer cuts all of his or her ties with his own army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. While they are part of an educational programme, they do severe all of their official ties -- not private ties. I believe that we are talking about the same things. I'm not talking about their private ties with their home country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you saying, General Skrbic, that if an officer in the Russian army is sent to school in the military education centre of the Army of Yugoslavia for a period of some months and in the middle of that period that Russian officer receives an order from his home army to return to the Russian army, that Russian officer does not have to obey that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are just assumptions, but I should say no. Education, Mr. Saxon, is usually carried out in peace time and there is never urgency for a person to go back home if they are in education, but the circumstances had changed. There was war going on and they were in education, and as such they were on the strength of the Army of Yugoslavia. We had students from Africa and they wore the uniforms of the Army of Yugoslavia when they were in education in Yugoslavia, and the same applied to officers of Republika Srpska, irrespective of the fact that they joined from the Army of Republika Srpska, they were members of the VJ while in education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- while you are ... Mr. Skrbic, during this time, during this war in the FRY, the bombing by NATO, were there any military students from France, Russia, and Africa in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Had there been any, would they have been assigned to go and do their work that the VRS members of the VJ contingent were assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't understand your question properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. You're discussing with Mr. Saxon that soldiers who were VRS soldiers but had come to school in the VJ were sent to war by you during 1999. Okay. That's what you are discussing. And you're saying -- your position is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- your position is such a student, while he's a student, he's part of the VJ and therefore he must carry out VJ orders. That's why they went. My question is: If at the time this bombardment took place you had soldiers from France, Russia, and Africa, would they also have been obliged to be ordered to go to war like the VRS was who were in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will give you a very specific example to illustrate my point, and I'm very familiar with that case. I spoke to General Talic, who at that moment was the Chief of Staff -- or rather, the Chief of the General Staff of the VRS. I asked him, "General, what are we supposed to do with the men in education?" And he said, "Skrbic, let them go to war. Those who do not want to go to war should not even return here once they finish with their education." That was our agreement and a decision was made. I was the one who proposed where those men should be sent, where they should be deployed, in view of their military specialties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Skrbic, for that explanation. Can I go back to my question. If at the time of the bombing by NATO you had in a VJ military school soldiers from Russia, France, and Africa, would you have ordered them also to go to war like you did soldiers from the Republika Srpska? Your answer doesn't have to be long. You can either say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence today, sir -- I'm from the United States, General Skrbic. Is it your evidence that if I had been a military officer from the United States and found myself studying for a year at the higher defence academy in Belgrade, that the Army of Yugoslavia could have ordered me to go to war and fight for Yugoslavia in war time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. In that case you would be fighting against yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Under what authority would the Army of Yugoslavia done that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't know the name of the officer from a higher -- a higher who is now in education at military academy. He is a member of the Army of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. My question wasn't clear. Under what legal authority would the Army of Yugoslavia have ordered me to fight for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the Law on Education and Scientific and Research institutions, which is currently in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would that -- was that law in effect in 1999?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question with a hundred per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you cite to us an article or section or chapter of that law that gives such authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, if the witness can't be sure whether the law existed, can he have a section and an article of the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about two different things. We're -- I'm not asking him now -- he mentioned a law. He's not sure when that law came into effect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- but I'm asking him whenever it came into effect, if he can take me to a particular portion or portions of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Saxon, I can't give you the exact portion of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you direct me to any portion of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia that grants such legal authority?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was the Law on Education, which is dedicated to education and scientific and research institutions and it stems from the basic Law on the Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which basic Law on the Military are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic Law on the Military of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This assessment that you received, your excellent assessment for this period in 1999 says that: "He," that's you, General Skrbic, "selected officers properly and quickly from the 30th Personnel Centre in order to dispatch them to units and installations." It doesn't say that you selected people from any military educational establishment. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I did not select people from that educational institution. There were people there from the entire state of Yugoslavia, from Yugoslavia, from Montenegro, from Serbia, and this document is worded the way it is to know exactly where I was proposing for them to be deployed to go into war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few moments ago we looked at the personnel file of Colonel Popovic, and we saw that he was assigned from the 30th Personnel Centre, that is, the Army of Republika Srpska, to the 2nd Army of the VJ during the Kosovo war. So Colonel Popovic was not in any educational establishment in the VJ when he was sent to the VJ 2nd Army; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not general, but colonel; and the answer is: No, he was not in any educational establishment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the Court's indulgence for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Skrbic, I would thank you for your time and your patience, and I'll pass you back to Mr. Lukic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I certainly cannot complete my additional examination today. If Mr. Skrbic is tired, could we perhaps be allowed not to begin within the next four or five minutes that we still have left today. You're probably going to ask me how much time I need for my additional questions. I have been notorious in my assessments not being correct. I believe that I could finish within one session. So as far as I'm concerned, I'm sure that Mr. Skrbic's testimony will be over today [as interpreted]. I can start now if Mr. Skrbic is not too tired, but I can't really cover any of the areas within the next three minutes to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you tired?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not, no, no. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you sure you're not tired? Okay. So the real reason is that you are not able to finish a point within the time remaining, not because he's tired? He hasn't complained. Okay. Then we'll stand adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00, Mr. Skrbic, not in the morning, it's quarter past 2.00; same court. Once again you are reminded not to discuss the case with anybody, especially not the Defence. Court adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just one small issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical issue. I don't know whether the Court can help me with that. General Skrbic before he came here to testify and when he came to testify, he applied to be able to visit two persons in the Detention Unit and he was told that he would be able to do that after the end of the testimony. Since we are in session tomorrow afternoon and it is possible that the Witness and Victims Unit will want to send him home on Wednesday morning, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to grant their approval for him to visit his friends tomorrow morning. I don't see any problem there, although his testimony is not finished, but he will certainly not be able to discuss any of the matters that are dealt with in his testimony because they would be under supervised visits. So I don't think there should be a problem with you granting him an approval to visit his friends tomorrow morning before the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you are standing up, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution feels that it would not be appropriate for General Skrbic to be meeting with his friends or former colleagues in the UN Detention Unit before his testimony is finished. There are just too many overlapping cases involved here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But apart from overlapping cases -- if you're using overlapping cases, that can still be affected even after he has testified. My answer to both of you is you are at the wrong forum. I am hearing -- this Chamber is hearing for the first time that Mr. Skrbic has asked for permission to go and visit his friends in the UNDU, and the authority that granted that permission and gave the condition that he does so after testifying is the correct authority that you must go to to ask for permission, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We stand adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.
